q: Two late-harvest categories were given legal force in 1984, ending a free-for-all in sweet-wine labelling. Which are they?
opts: Vendanges Tardives and Selection de Grains Nobles
exp: The 1984 decree fixed minimum must weights, banned any addition of sugar and required hand picking. Before it, a grower could put almost any word on a rich wine.

q: A grower has beautifully botrytised Sylvaner and wants to bottle it as Selection de Grains Nobles. What stands in the way?
opts: Sylvaner is incapable of developing noble rot
Only the four noble varieties may carry the term
Sylvaner may only be used at Grand Cru level
The wine would have to be sold as Cremant instead
exp: Selection de Grains Nobles is restricted to Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, and Vendanges Tardives is confined to the same four grapes. Sylvaner does raisin and rot in a warm autumn, but it may carry neither late-harvest term.

q: Vendanges Tardives and Selection de Grains Nobles both set minimum must weights, and for two of the four permitted grapes the bar is higher. Which pair faces it?
exp: Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris accumulate sugar far more readily, so the law asks more of them before the same words may be used. Riesling and Muscat qualify at a lower level of ripeness.

q: Pickers go through the rows several times over weeks, taking only shrivelled, fungus-affected berries. Which category demands that?
exp: Selection de Grains Nobles requires noble rot and berry-by-berry selection across successive passes. Vendanges Tardives asks only for late picking, with botrytis permitted rather than required.

q: A wine labelled Vendanges Tardives goes to a guest who is expecting a dessert wine. What should the server flag first?
opts: It may be rich but close to dry
It will have been fortified with grape spirit
It will always be sweeter than a Selection de Grains Nobles
exp: The category sets a minimum sugar level in the fruit at picking, not in the finished wine. A producer is free to ferment that sugar out, and some celebrated examples are nearly dry.

q: Adding sugar to the must is forbidden outright for Vendanges Tardives and Selection de Grains Nobles alike. Why does that ban matter?
opts: Added sugar would halt the fermentation prematurely
The wines are fermented without cultured yeast
Chaptalisation is illegal everywhere in France
The vine, not the cellar, must do the work
exp: The whole claim of a late-harvest wine is that the concentration happened on the vine. Chaptalisation is permitted for ordinary Alsace, which is what gives the prohibition teeth here: the sugar has to come from hanging time and noble rot, not from a sack in the cellar.

q: Vendanges Tardives and Selection de Grains Nobles may not be released for some time after the harvest. For roughly how long?
exp: The wines may not be sold until eighteen months have passed, which lets them settle and lets the authorities taste them. Both categories must also pass an official tasting before the term is granted.

q: Second fermentation in the bottle, whole-bunch pressing and nine months on the lees define the region's sparkling appellation, created in 1976. Which is it?
exp: It is made by the same traditional method as Champagne, from hand-picked fruit pressed in whole bunches. Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois form the backbone of most cuvees.

q: One grape is authorised in the region for sparkling wine alone and may never appear in a still Alsace bottling. Which?
exp: Chardonnay is permitted solely for Cremant d'Alsace, where its acidity and neutrality suit a base wine. As a still varietal it would simply compete with the region's own identity.

q: A pink Cremant d'Alsace must be made from one variety and one only. Which?
exp: Cremant d'Alsace Rose is entirely Pinot Noir, taken from the skins by pressing or short maceration. Blending finished red wine into white to make the colour is not allowed.

q: A blended white sold under an Alsatian word meaning noble mixture may draw on any permitted white grape in any proportion. Which term?
exp: Edel means noble and zwicker means blend, though in practice this is the everyday carafe wine of the region. No minimum proportion of the noble grapes applies, and a vintage is optional.

q: A stricter blend term requires at least half the wine to come from the noble varieties, each vinified separately, with a vintage on the label. Which term?
exp: Gentil sets a floor of fifty percent Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris or Gewurztraminer, insists each component would qualify as Alsace in its own right, and sends the finished wine to a tasting panel.

q: A tall, slender green bottle is compulsory for the region's still wines, which must also be bottled inside the region. What is that bottle called?
exp: The flute, sometimes called the vin du Rhin bottle, is written into law along with the requirement to bottle locally. Between them they make an Alsace bottle recognisable across a dining room.

q: Naming the grape on the front label is the rule here and the exception in France. What must a varietal Alsace wine contain?
opts: At least half of the named variety
All of the named variety and nothing else
At least eighty-five percent of the named variety
At least seventy-five percent of the named variety
exp: There is no blending allowance whatsoever: a wine sold as Riesling is Riesling entire. The apparent exceptions are naming conventions rather than blends, since Muscat covers both permitted Muscats and Pinot Blanc may be Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois or the two together.

q: A label reads Reserve, or Cuvee Speciale, and offers nothing further. What weight should that carry?
opts: None in law, since such terms are unregulated here
It guarantees at least two years in barrel
It marks a Grand Cru site left unnamed on the label
exp: These are house words with no legal definition in Alsace. The claims that mean something are the appellation, the named site, the variety, the vintage and the two late-harvest terms.

q: Within a few kilometres a grower may work granite, sandstone, limestone, marl, schist and volcanic rock. What produced that jumble?
opts: River silt laid down over successive floods
Ash from an extinct chain of volcanoes
Glaciers grinding down a single limestone plateau
exp: The Rhine valley collapsed along a fault line and the western shoulder was tilted and shattered, exposing rock of wildly different ages side by side. Around a dozen distinct soil types are recognised.
